evidence_items.content: Demographics: 59-year-old woman
Chief complaint: 2 days of left orbital pain
Medical history: hypertension controlled with lisinopril
Medical history: several months of epiphora without prior dacryocystitis
Visual acuity: 20/25 OD and 20/400 OS
Edematous, hyperemic left eyelids
Diffuse limitation in extraocular movements in the left eye
Normal intraocular pressure
Normal fundi on both sides
Imaging: Coronal Computed Tomography Scan showed left-sided lacrimal sac abscess
Imaging: postseptal fat stranding largely limited to the extraconal space
Imaging: minimal sinus mucosal thickening
Imaging: opacification of both nasolacrimal ducts
Imaging: Repeat Contrast-Enhanced Computed Tomography showed increased abscess size with globe compression
Imaging: minimal intraconal fat stranding
Imaging: unremarkable optic nerve appearance on follow-up CT
Imaging: Magnetic Resonance Imaging and Angiography showed patent ophthalmic artery
Imaging: diffusion-weighted imaging showed acute injury to the entire orbital segment of the left optic nerve
Laboratory: Initial cultures isolated gram-positive cocci in chains
Laboratory: later identified as pan-susceptible Streptococcus pyogenes

evidence_items.content: Demographics: female patient in her early 50s
Chief complaint: multiple bluish, partially keratotic papules and nodules on the lower legs
Number of lesions: approximately 10
Lesion characteristics: bluish, partially keratotic papules and nodules
Lesion location: lower legs
Lesion growth: very slow in number and size since age 24
Lesion bleeding: occasional after trauma
Mobility aid: wheelchair due to right-sided hemiparesis and hemianopsia
Cause of hemiparesis and hemianopsia: intracranial hemorrhage
History of seizures: recurrent seizures at age 4
Lipolymphedema: present in the lower legs
Lipolymphedema cause: functional venous insufficiency with insufficient venous pump activity

cases.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
cases.vignette: A female patient in her early 50s presented with multiple (approximately 10) bluish, partially keratotic papules and nodules on the lower legs. The lesions had been growing very slowly in number and size since age 24 and had been bleeding occasionally after trauma. The patient used a wheelchair due to right-sided hemiparesis and hemianopsia caused by an intracranial hemorrhage. At age 4, she had recurrent seizures. She had lipolymphedema of the lower legs attributed to functional venous insufficiency with insufficient venous pump activity, and had been wearing compression stockings for years. Family history revealed similar conditions in the patient's father and aunt, with the father having died of an intracranial hemorrhage in his early 70s. Multiple bluish, partially keratotic papules and nodules on the lower legs. Lipolymphedema of the lower legs was present. Right-sided hemiparesis and hemianopsia were noted. - Sonography: Demonstrated intradermal slow-flow vascular malformations with a maximum diameter of 1.2 cm. - Histopathology: Image Description: Biopsy revealed a well-circumscribed lesion with hyperkeratosis and acanthosis of the epidermis overlying a conglomerate of dilated venous-like malformations with continuous smooth muscle in the upper dermis, partly showing thrombosis. - Genetic Testing: Result: Detection of a heterozygous pathogenic KRIT1 variant.

evidence_items.content: Demographics: female patient in her late 20s
Chief complaint: 2-year history of multiple, slowly growing, infiltrated erythematous-violaceous patches and plaques
Location of patches and plaques: left upper arm to the left side of her chest
Symptoms: occasional slight pain
No triggers such as local infection, insect bite, or trauma occurred before lesion appearance
Denied fever, weight loss, or fatigue
Multiple firm, nonscaly, purple erythematous patches and plaques with irregular borders on her left axilla, medial upper arm, and lateral thoracic region
No extracutaneous involvement was observed
Histopathological examination: thin-walled, irregularly branched blood vessels dispersed between thickened collagen bundles
Endothelial cells were plump but displayed no significant cytologic atypia
Immunohistochemistry results: positive for CD31, CD34, Ki-67 (<1%)
Immunohistochemistry results: negative for podoplanin (D2-40), human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)

cases.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
cases.vignette:
A female patient in her late 20s presented with a 2-year history of multiple, slowly growing, infiltrated erythematous-violaceous patches and plaques, with occasional slight pain extending from her left upper arm to the left side of her chest. No triggers such as local infection, insect bite, or trauma occurred before lesion appearance. She denied fever, weight loss, or fatigue.

Multiple firm, nonscaly, purple erythematous patches and plaques with irregular borders on her left axilla, medial upper arm, and lateral thoracic region. No extracutaneous involvement was observed.

- Histopathological examination:    - Thin-walled, irregularly branched blood vessels dispersed between thickened collagen bundles    - Endothelial cells were plump but displayed no significant cytologic atypia      - Immunohistochemistry results:    - Positive for: CD31, CD34, Ki-67 (<1%)    - Negative for: podoplanin (D2-40), human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)      - Images:    Image A Title: Clinical presentation    Image A Description: Multiple nonscaly, erythematous-violaceous patches and plaques with irregular borders on the patient's left axilla, medial upper arm, and lateral thoracic region        Image B Title: Histopathological examination (hematoxylin-eosin)    Image B Description: Irregularly branched, thin-walled blood vessels dissecting through collagen bundles within the superficial to mid dermis        Image C Title: Detailed histopathology (hematoxylin-eosin)    Image C Description: Irregularly branched, thin-walled blood vessels with plump endothelial cells dispersed between thickened collagen bundles without signs of atypia        Image D Title: Immunohistochemistry    Image D Description: Endothelial cells positive for cluster of differentiation (CD) 31

cases.vignette:
An 11-year-old boy presented with progressive unilateral skin hardening on his right thigh and buttock for 7 years. Recently, the motion of his right limb joint was slightly limited. He was born to healthy parents and did not have any medical disease.

There was an ill-defined, stony-hard plaque involving his right thigh above the patella extending to his right buttocks with loss of skin elasticity. The affected skin was associated with mild hypertrichosis and hyperpigmentation.

- Laboratory tests: Normal results for routine blood tests, autoantibodies, immunoglobulins, C-reactive protein, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate.- Imaging studies:  Image Title: MRI of right thigh  Image Description: Demonstrated slight thickening of subcutaneous tissue and T2 signal abnormality- Pathological examination:  - Histopathological findings: Normal epidermis and mild pigmentation along the basal layer with subtle increase in density of fibroblasts extending to the subcutis and forming adipocyte entrapment but no evidence of inflammation. Dense reticular dermis extended below well-preserved appendages  - Immunohistochemical staining: Increased expression of CD34 in the reticular dermis  - Alcian blue staining: Negative
